econ.analysis: This week is the first where the data has caught up to the escalation rather than lagging behind it. Kpler's confirmation that strait traffic fell 28% to its lowest since May validates what independent analysts were already flagging days ago — the optimistic 'recovering to two-thirds of pre-war' narrative from late August has not survived contact with a week of destroyed tankers. The one genuine counter-signal is DII buying holding up even as FIIs turned sellers, suggesting domestic conviction that this repricing is a buying opportunity rather than the start of a deeper rout — but that's a bet on this week being the peak, not a certainty.

hormuzEvents.e: DAY 195 — TEN STRIKES EACH WAY, AND THE FIRST REPORTED TANKER-CREW DEATH OF THE WEEK. Wire reporting through Sept 9-10 puts the week's tally at ten Iranian tankers struck by the US (up from the eight confirmed Tuesday) and ten vessels struck by Iran near the strait — the most intense single week of tanker warfare since the conflict began. The IRGC added a new threat: expanding its maritime exclusion zone toward Chabahar, on Iran's southeastern coast outside the strait itself. DAY 194 — VERIFIED DATA CATCHES UP TO THE ESCALATION. The IRGC attempted to hit a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the two days prior; the warship evaded both attempts, no Americans harmed. CENTCOM retaliated Tuesday by destroying five more Iranian crude carriers — M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar and M/T Horizon 1 (Aframax, oil/chemical and LPG tankers respectively) and M/T Riesco in the Gulf of Oman, plus M/T Derya near Kharg Island — directing crews to abandon ship before the strikes. That brings the week's total to eight Iranian tankers destroyed or disabled. Secretary of State Rubio, in Colombia: "Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers." In response, the IRGC Navy warned all oil tanker crews near the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain to evacuate their vessels immediately, threatening to target ships there for hosting US forces. Iran separately claimed a strike on Jordan's Al-Azraq air base, targeting a fighter-jet hangar; a US official called it 'ineffective.' Trump said oil prices will drop "when we WIN the war." Iran's Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran is preparing a restricted zone in the Persian Gulf and threatened a full blockade in and around Hormuz over US sanctions — a harder line than his 'new shipping route' framing from two days earlier. Qatar's Foreign Ministry warned of an 'industrial catastrophe' if the crisis continues, citing Kpler data showing strait traffic fell 28% last week to 77 vessels, roughly 10-11 ships a day — the lowest level since May, confirming independent analysts' earlier, more pessimistic throughput estimates over Washington's own figures. Brent hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May, amid reports that Iran-backed Houthi attacks disrupted Saudi energy infrastructure. India's markets fell for a third consecutive session: Sensex down 813.35 points (-1.08%) to 74,764.23, Nifty down 203.60 points (-0.86%) to 23,431.50, with IT and realty stocks leading losses. FIIs turned net sellers (-₹123 crore Tuesday); DIIs kept buying (+₹1,349.64 crore). India's defence stocks gained after the government approved roughly $11 billion in military purchases.

DAY 192 — A NEW ROUTE OFFERED, A HARDER LINE THREATENED. Iran's top security official Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran will declare a restricted zone near the Strait of Hormuz and announce a new shipping route agreed with Oman "in the coming days" — a genuine softening from his own position a week earlier, when he said the strait 'will not reopen' while US forces remain in the Gulf. The same day, Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned of a "heavier and more painful response" to any new US attacks, directly referencing Saturday's destruction of the tanker M/T Kylo and disabling of two more vessels. Separately, USNI News reported that Chris Newton, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, estimates actual Hormuz crude flow in August was around 5-7 million barrels a day — an improving trend, but well below the 10 million bpd average (up to 15-17 million on a single day) that Treasury Secretary Bessent has cited, a reminder that official throughput figures from either government warrant scrutiny. Iran struck at least 13 commercial vessels in August. India's markets, closed all weekend, open today for the first time since Saturday's tanker-sinking escalation; Nifty enters the session on its longest weekly losing streak in five months, having gained just 0.10% Friday on dovish Fed commentary. Analysts have flagged the weekend's US-Iran escalation as the key uncertain variable for today's trade, with support at 23,780-23,830 and resistance at 24,000-24,050.

DAY 191 — THE US SINKS AN IRANIAN TANKER FOR THE FIRST TIME. The IRGC fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and a guided-missile destroyer patrolling regional waters on Saturday; both evaded the attacks and no American personnel were harmed, though the targeting of a carrier itself is a notable provocation. CENTCOM retaliated under a 'tanker for tanker' policy Trump approved earlier in the month — first used September 1-2 against two Iranian government tankers, and now expanded further: US forces permanently disabled the crude carriers M/T Downy off Kharg Island and M/T Stark 1 near Jask, and completely destroyed the unladen M/T Kylo ('Noxen') in the Gulf of Oman, directing its crew to abandon ship before multiple strikes rendered it inoperable. CENTCOM described the three vessels as part of a 'multibillion-dollar shadow network' funding the IRGC. Adm. Brad Cooper: "If you shoot at two of our ships, we will impose an even higher economic cost — taking out three of yours. We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran's limited and exposed oil fleet." Iran's IRGC Navy separately claimed to have targeted three tankers on an 'unauthorized route' and three US-affiliated vessels elsewhere — an unconfirmed Iranian claim. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya central command warned that continued 'harassment' and naval blockade would trigger attacks 'more severe than before' with a 'possibility of their expansion.' Trump, by contrast, called the war 'small potatoes' and 'not a big thing,' saying the US has 'essentially' taken over Iran. Dubai crude jumped to near $100 a barrel, the highest since May, as Indian and Chinese refiners intensified spot-market purchases of Middle East crude, competing directly with South Korean and Japanese buyers. The Institute for the Study of War's Critical Threats Project assessed Iran has not achieved its core Hormuz objective and may be waiting for a more advantageous moment to escalate further, consistent with a New York Times report that US intelligence assesses Iran 'may be considering a significant escalation.' Separately, Qatar's Foreign Ministry issued the first Gulf-state rebuttal of Iran's claim that its strikes are purely defensive, citing UN-documented Iranian strikes on civilian and commercial sites in Qatar; Doha stressed it remains 'not party to the conflict' and continues mediating with Pakistan and Oman. Indian markets are closed for the weekend; Friday's close was Sensex 76,645.88 (+493.02, +0.65%), Nifty 23,937.90 (+64.45, +0.27%), snapping a four-day losing streak on Fed rate relief even as Brent/Dubai crude rose toward its strongest weekly gain since mid-July.

DAY 189 — A CORRECTION, A CONFIRMATION, AND A QUIET DIPLOMATIC TRACK. Iran's own Red Crescent Society revised the toll from the September 1 Sirik wedding strike sharply down: four people killed (two women, two children) and more than 60 wounded — a marked reduction from Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei's earlier claim of 50+ casualties. CENTCOM's Capt. Tim Hawkins said the US military was "looking into" the reports without confirming a formal investigation. Vice President JD Vance told reporters he was "extremely skeptical" of the claim, citing Iranian state media's unreliable record through the conflict, and repeatedly declined to call the overall situation a "war," saying the US would rely on its own tools rather than depend on Iran "behaving responsibly." Separately, Saudi Arabia's national carrier Bahri confirmed two Filipino seafarers were killed when its tanker MV Sidr was struck transiting Hormuz on Monday night — independently verified casualties, distinct from either government's disputed claims. Iran struck Kuwait and Bahrain with drones for a second consecutive night; Kuwait's Ministry of Defense called it "blatant Iranian aggression." Iran's army claimed a third night of attacks on bases used by US forces in Kuwait and the UAE, and disclosed its own losses from the September 1-2 exchange: four IRGC Aerospace Force personnel, two navy members, and one Basij militia member killed. Iran blacklisted 11 more ships, bringing its Hormuz blacklist to 56 vessels. Behind the public escalation, Reuters reported that senior Trump aides are working to prevent further escalation before the US midterm elections, with officials expected to weigh additional military action afterward; Special Envoy Steve Witkoff held a previously unannounced meeting with the UAE's national security adviser in Sardinia to discuss next steps, first reported by Axios. India's markets rallied sharply: the Sensex rose 504 points and the Nifty moved back above 23,900, as easing US bond-yield pressure and a tech-led Wall Street rally improved the global risk mood.

DAY 187 — THE MOST SERIOUS ESCALATION SINCE THE WAR'S MIDPOINT. US Central Command said late Tuesday it had completed a wave of strikes against IRGC targets "including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites," citing recent attempted IRGC attacks on shipping and American personnel. Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm Island, in Konarak and in Chabahar. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei claimed the strikes hit a residential home in Kuhestak, Sirik, during a wedding celebration, with more than 50 people killed or wounded — a serious allegation from the Iranian government that has not been independently verified; CENTCOM's own statement named target classes, not this site. Baqaei vowed a firm response to what he called "savage crimes." Iran's IRNA separately claimed retaliatory strikes on Jordan's Prince Hassan Air Base and Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, also unconfirmed by third parties. The IRGC warned its "offensive operation will continue," and Trump warned Iran would be hit "harder" if it retaliates further. At the G20 finance ministers' meeting, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Strait of Hormuz will become a "worthless piece of water" within two years as Gulf oil shifts to land pipelines, a long-horizon claim that sits oddly alongside the day's active combat. Markets reacted sharply: the Sensex opened down 472.96 points (-0.61%) to 76,471.32 and the Nifty fell 196.60 points to 23,859.20, as Japan's Nikkei fell 2.9% and Korea's Kospi 3.1%, and the US 10-year Treasury yield hit 4.81%, its highest since late 2023. Brent traded above $92 with diesel crack spreads breaching $100. The rupee was the one bright spot, opening at a two-month high of ₹94.91 on strong 7.8% India GDP data and returning FII/DII buying.

DAY 186 — ATTACKS, THREATS, AND AN OPENING, ALL IN ONE DAY. The Larak Island exchange that broke a month-long lull kept unfolding through Tuesday. Two more tankers — a South Korean-owned vessel and a Saudi-flagged ship — were struck by unknown projectiles Monday evening while transiting Hormuz's southern corridor, the route the Trump administration had specifically called safe; UKMTO reported one hit by three projectiles 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, Oman. Trump said the US would hit Iran "hard" over its Jordan attacks, but downplayed a return to full-scale war when asked directly, calling Iran a "failed nation." Axios reported that Trump and senior aides had spent the past week weighing a CENTCOM-developed plan for further limited strikes to prevent Iran reconstituting its radar and missile capabilities — a plan not approved before Sunday's Larak Island strike happened regardless. Vice President Vance said Trump's AI-generated Truth Social video of Kharg Island being destroyed was intended as a message to Tehran, while stressing Trump wouldn't announce real military actions on social media. Set against all of that: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan alongside Russia's Putin, China's Xi and India's Modi, said Iran would "immediately reciprocate" with free Hormuz navigation if the US restores its June memorandum of understanding commitments — the most concrete conditional offer either side has made in weeks. Iran's central bank governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said Iran has sufficient FX reserves despite sanctions and is ready to inject up to $2bn to calm currency volatility. India's markets absorbed the day's whiplash better than the morning suggested: after GIFT Nifty pointed to a weak open and the Sensex fell as much as 231 points intraday, strong GDP data and a likely RBI intervention helped both indices close only marginally lower — Sensex -12.99 (-0.02%) to 76,944.28, Nifty -24.60 (-0.10%) to 24,055.80 — a second straight losing session, but a far smaller one than the morning's escalation implied. Brent held above $90.

DAY 185 — THE MARKET REACTS AFTER ALL. Monday's calm, coiled pre-market open didn't hold: by 11am the Sensex had fallen 483 points (-0.63%) to 76,781 and the Nifty 171 points (-0.71%) to 24,004, as rising oil prices and concern about a US Federal Reserve rate hike dented risk sentiment — the first real market reaction since the weekend's CENTCOM-IRGC rhetorical exchange, even if the actual driver was more about oil direction and Fed policy than the Hormuz dispute itself. Two independent data points arrived to fill the information gap the rhetoric left behind. Goldman Sachs estimated Gulf oil exports have recovered to roughly two-thirds of pre-war levels — 15-16 million barrels a day, up from a March trough of 5-6 million but still 7-8 million below pre-conflict volumes. Reuters' own ship-tracking counted just 10 visible commodity-vessel transits through the strait on August 26, below the 10-day moving average of about 15. Separately, an analysis by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) found the Hormuz crisis has added an estimated $22 billion to India's gross fossil-fuel import costs between March and August — India was the second-most affected importer after China in gross terms, with a net additional cost of $14.4 billion across all fuels (about 0.38% of GDP) and $20.5 billion on crude oil alone. CREA also found the import-parity cost of a standard 14.2kg LPG cylinder rose roughly 29% since the war began. CENTCOM and Iran continue to dispute control of the strait without new claims from either side since Saturday.

DAY 184 — THE REBUTTAL. Two days after CENTCOM and Trump declared Hormuz's mines cleared and the strait effectively open, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy issued a direct, sharply worded rejection: "the control exercised by the Islamic Republic's forces over the strategic Strait of Hormuz is complete and decisive," it said, calling US claims "an outright lie" intended "solely to control oil prices and cover up their own defeats." The statement said the strait remains closed to any vessel transiting without prior coordination with Iran, a condition that holds until US "aggression" ends and outstanding obligations under the Islamabad memorandum are fulfilled. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said separately that the temporary arrangement reached with Oman depends entirely on Washington restoring commitments it has suspended: "if they take no action, then naturally the Islamic Republic is in no hurry to reopen the Strait of Hormuz." He also rejected reports that vessels had transited without Iranian coordination. Former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei took the hardest public line yet, saying the strait "will not reopen" unless American forces withdraw from the Gulf entirely. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei urged Muslim heads of state to "recognise their real enemy," and Iran's Cabinet pledged to stand firm against US sanctions as the war passed its six-month mark. Israeli strikes wounded several in central Gaza; a "massive" explosion was reported in southern Lebanon. India's markets remain closed for the weekend, with Monday's reopening the first real test of how seriously markets take Tehran's rebuttal.

DAY 183 — THE US CALLS IT OPEN. CENTCOM chief Admiral Brad Cooper said in a video statement that internationally recognised sea routes in the Strait of Hormuz are free of Iranian sea mines, calling it a "major milestone." Hours later Trump told Axios in a phone interview, "that sucker is open. The Iranian response is very mild. They don't want us to go back at them. That's the whole ball game." US officials say 20 to 30 tankers are now transiting the strait nightly, roughly half the pre-war rate, with Iran striking only about 2% of ships that transited over the past month; Kpler shipping data logged seven commodity vessels transiting Thursday against a 10-day average of 15. Trump wrote on Truth Social that he isn't interested in negotiating further — "I don't want to meet, they do... they are begging to make a deal" — and that June's memorandum of understanding is no longer relevant. Iran's military separately reached a narrower revenue-sharing agreement with Oman over the strait, though Tehran stressed this does not guarantee full reopening. Brent steadied near $88, roughly flat on the week, as Hormuz optimism met a new risk from an escalating Russia-Ukraine war. India's Sensex rose 331 points (+0.43%) on an IT-led rally Friday to close at 77,265, even as the index ended the week 0.4% lower; Indian markets are closed for the weekend, with trading resuming Monday, September 1.

DAY 181 — THE OMAN DEAL, RECONSIDERED. Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said the framework Tehran and Muscat outlined a day earlier would in fact see the closure of the southern shipping route — the UN-authorised lane along Oman's coast that Iran has long opposed — rather than reopening the strait, according to state-linked Press TV; Oman's own statement had not mentioned any closure. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he told Trump a diplomatic deal with Iran is "not possible," calling its leadership "savages." Trump told Al Jazeera the US is "achieving a very big victory" and the war "will continue for as long as necessary," with no timetable for talks to resume. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told counterparts the US is not planning new strikes "for the time being," leaning on sanctions instead while keeping retaliation on the table. Iranian official Mohebbi claimed the strait is under Iran's control with US warships 250 miles away; CNN reported experts doubt Iran's ability to actually clear mines. Regional reporting described a "busy day" of 20 tanker transfers moving oil out of Gulf states excluding Iran. Brent held near $85.5, a fourth straight session of declines. India's Sensex and Nifty gave back Wednesday's morning gains to close lower, while GIFT Nifty pointed to a firmer Thursday open and the rupee was set to strengthen after Wednesday's currency-market holiday.

DAY 180 — TWO CLAIMS, ONE STRAIT. Trump said on Truth Social that the US Navy had cleared or detonated all mines from the international waters of the Strait of Hormuz, covering both the inbound and outbound lanes of the main shipping corridor, and warned that any vessel laying new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed" under a zero-tolerance policy. CENTCOM said more than 500 ships had transited the southern lane in the past 30 days with roughly 2% struck. Hours later, Oman's foreign minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi and Iran's Abbas Araghchi announced a phased framework for a temporary joint navigational corridor — inbound through Iranian waters, outbound through Iranian or Omani waters, commercial vessels only, no warships — alongside a joint mine-clearance project, with a permanent route to be negotiated within 30-60 days. Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi said this does not amount to reopening the strait, which he said remains closed until Washington meets Tehran's conditions. Trump told Al Jazeera he was "not in a hurry" on talks with Iran and that both economic and military pressure "are effective." Brent extended its slide to a third session, falling more than 2% to around $86.5. Iran separately blacklisted 45 ships accused of ship-to-ship transfers evading its own blockade. Indian markets were shut for currency and debt trading on account of Eid-e-Milad, though equities remained open; GIFT Nifty pointed to a higher start after Tuesday's gains.

DAY 179 — DIPLOMACY RESUMES AND THE PRICE FALLS. Oman's foreign minister Sayyid Badr al-Busaidi travelled to Tehran for talks on the Strait of Hormuz and other regional developments, days after President Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it obstructed US efforts; no outcome was announced. Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, was in Tehran the same day and was photographed reviewing a map of the strait with interior minister Eskandar Momeni, having been told by security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei that Washington must take concrete steps to fulfil the June memorandum. Iran's assembly advanced plans for Hormuz service fees. Brent fell more than 3% to around $89.26 with an intraday low of $87.65, as traders judged Monday's sanctions to pose less risk to oil supply than military escalation would. Iran's national police chief warned that adversaries were seeking to exploit grievances over livelihoods, petrol and unemployment to trigger unrest, and the US State Department offered up to $10 million for information on five senior IRGC commanders. Saudi shipping company Bahri said one of its tankers was involved in a security incident in the Red Sea after a claimed Houthi missile attack.

DAY 178 — OPERATION ECONOMIC OUTCAST BEGINS, AND STOPS SHORT. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced at a Washington news conference that the United States had begun an unprecedented campaign against Iran and its enablers, designating roughly 60 entities, individuals and vessels involved in illicit procurement of nuclear and missile technology, cyber operations and oil smuggling, and naming a network of brokers, companies and shadow-fleet vessels operating across the UAE, Hong Kong, China, Singapore, Switzerland and Europe to transport Iranian oil and channel revenue to the IRGC-Qods Force. Secondary sanction categories were widened to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping, and several licences permitting payments to Iran and Iranian access to US cultural and academic institutions were suspended. But no country was named for secondary penalties and no timeline given; Bessent called it a warning shot, said everyone was being given the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour, and argued that total financial isolation could make US force unnecessary. The rial fell to a record 2.02 million to the dollar. Iran's finance minister said Tehran had a two-year plan and would not respond purely defensively; parliament speaker Ghalibaf conceded that Iran could not endure if its people went hungry. Oman's foreign minister travels to Tehran on Tuesday.

DAY 175-177 — SELECTIVE ACCESS OPENS AS TEHRAN THREATENS THIRD COUNTRIES. Reuters confirmed, citing Iranian state news agency IRNA, that Iran is allowing some Iraqi oil tankers through the strait — the first country-specific exemption of the war, granted after Baghdad requested special status. Analysis of UK maritime agency figures put ship numbers at about 20% of the pre-war average, with more than 80% of liquids over the past fortnight using the UN-authorised Omani channel rather than the Iranian-designated route, and the US military said it had escorted more than 660 million barrels since early May, some tankers running with transponders off. Reuters nonetheless described shipments as at a virtual standstill, with Tehran threatening to strike unauthorised tankers. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, declared that any country joining the US economic war would be considered an enemy and warned neighbours that cooperation would see their interests targeted, while raising the prospect of halting oil flows; Iran's foreign ministry called the sanctions a declaration of war on all nations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote in the Financial Times that an economic D-Day was coming, ahead of a Monday news conference. President Pezeshkian said Iran cannot continue with war forever.

DAY 171-175 — THE NEGOTIATING WINDOW EXPIRES AND THE ECONOMIC WAR WIDENS. The 60-day period agreed in June ran out on Monday 17 August with no agreement. Iran's foreign ministry said it had reached an arrangement with Oman on future shipping routes — vessels entering through Iranian waters and exiting through Omani waters, described by Tehran as a new security model rather than a reopening — and President Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way", objecting to joint Iranian-Omani management of the exit route. In the Oval Office he called making the strait a US territory "a great idea", saying "we control it with the blockade". On Tuesday he said no talks were underway; Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf issued a list of demands for reopening. On Thursday Washington announced a sweeping package to cut Iran off from international banks, businesses, shipping registries, cash transfers and smuggling networks, alongside new sanctions on Hezbollah, and the UAE suspended financial and economic transactions with Iran after accusing Tehran of firing ballistic missiles at its territory. Brent rose through the week to around $93. Iraq has asked Iran to grant special status to its oil exports through the strait.

DAY 173-174 — ECONOMIC D-DAY. President Trump announced a "crushing economic operation" against Iran consisting of "Economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale", warning that any country allowing its financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran would itself face tremendous economic consequences. He specified oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies, adding "You know who you are", and called on allies to help isolate and defeat Iran. The United Arab Emirates suspended trade with Iran after coming under renewed missile fire. US officials said Trump had threatened to bomb Oman because he was unhappy with the Strait of Hormuz deal Muscat was working out with Tehran. Brent traded near $92 and WTI above $85, the highest of the war. Kpler reported Bab el-Mandeb crossings up 6.7% to 254 transits with dark transits down from 40 to 16, while Hormuz traffic stayed in single figures. France announced it would expel two Iranian diplomats.

DAY 172-173 — WASHINGTON CLAIMS THE WATERWAY, TEHRAN CLAIMS A DEAL WITH MUSCAT. President Trump posted a map labelling the Strait of Hormuz as "new" United States territory, following his statement last week that he would declare it American territory once Iran is defeated. He rejected any extension of the memorandum that expired on Monday, said no talks were taking place, and signalled that the blockade on Iranian shipping would be reinstated; US strikes on Iran resumed overnight. Iran's foreign ministry accused Washington of squeezing Tehran for concessions and reiterated that it will not negotiate directly with the United States, while stating that it had reached an agreement with Oman on future shipping routes through the strait. A regional source told CNN the two expect to reach a middle ground on managing the waterway within days. Brent broke $91 and WTI topped $85. CENTCOM said it had redirected 64 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two as of 17 August, and Iran denied claims that it had fired missiles at the United Arab Emirates.

DAY 171-172 — THE FRAMEWORK EXPIRES AND THE MEDIATOR IS THREATENED. The 60-day memorandum signed at Versailles on 17 June lapsed on Monday with no successor deal and without a single major commercial tanker route restored. Under its terms the United States was to end its naval blockade within 30 days, withdraw forces near Iran after a final deal, lift sanctions, issue waivers for Iranian oil exports, allow access to frozen funds and begin a reconstruction package of at least $300bn, while Iran was to clear mines and allow vessels to pass without charge for 60 days. Trump had declared it over within a month. Asked in the Oval Office whether he had run out of patience with Oman, the President said "I don't think they behaved very well, but we'd handle them very easily", after telling a Fox News correspondent the United States would bomb Oman if it got in the way of reopening the strait. Kpler recorded five commodity vessels crossing on Saturday and none on Sunday, against 31 the previous weekend. Al Arabiya reported a ceasefire extension had been agreed; a senior Iranian official denied any such talks.

DAY 170-171 — THE MEMORANDUM EXPIRES AND TRANSITS REACH ZERO. The 60-day memorandum of understanding signed on 17 June by Donald Trump and Masoud Pezeshkian, following high-level talks hosted by Pakistan, expired on Monday with no deal and no replacement. Under its terms the United States was to lift the naval blockade within 30 days and, on reaching a final agreement, withdraw its forces, lift sanctions, grant exemptions for Iranian oil exports, restore access to frozen funds and prepare a reconstruction and development package worth at least $300 billion; Iran was to clear the strait of mines and ensure free passage for 60 days. Both sides alleged violations within ten days, and Trump declared the agreement over on 7 July. Kpler tracking reported by Reuters recorded no transits whatsoever through the strait on Sunday. Iran's army chief, Major General Amir Hatami, announced a reward of about 5 billion tomans, roughly $30,000, for any Iranian who captures or kills a US service member. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiations cannot resume until Washington ends its violations and compensates Iran, and that the Oman understanding does not by itself reopen the waterway.

DAY 168-170 — TRANSITS COLLAPSE TOWARDS ZERO AS TANKER ATTACKS MOUNT. The United Arab Emirates said Iran attacked two vessels affiliated with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company as they transited the strait on Thursday evening, and ADNOC reported a third attacked on Friday evening — the third incident involving its tankers in 48 hours, after three earlier attacks days before. The UK Maritime Trade Operations reported two nearly identical drone strikes causing minor damage and, on Saturday, an unknown projectile striking the hull of a bulk carrier. Kpler vessel-tracking data indicated traffic slowed dramatically on Friday, with only two non-oil vessels crossing and no crude shipments visible. President Trump said he would "pretty soon" declare the strait a territory of the United States once Iran is defeated, offering no legal mechanism; Iran's deputy foreign minister Kazem Gharibabadi replied that it cannot be seized by tweet, aircraft carrier, order or election speech and will remain Iranian. The Gulf Cooperation Council, Qatar, Bahrain and Egypt condemned the attacks, with Doha rejecting the use of the strait as leverage and demanding unconditional reopening. Iran and Oman have still not agreed terms.

DAY 168-169 — PRESSURE TIGHTENS, AND THE PRICE FOLLOWS. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Newsmax that Washington would pursue the "economic isolation" of Iran with measures that "have never been seen", with further announcements expected next week, a day after Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said the naval blockade of Iranian ports could be maintained indefinitely by rotating ships. Brent closed Friday at $88.52, up 1.7%, and more than 5% on the week; WTI settled at $82.40. The IEA warned that renewed hostilities threaten to push the market into its widest supply deficit in five years, with supply falling 4.3 million barrels a day across 2026. Iran and Oman have still not agreed terms for reopening the strait, which Washington has said would be the trigger for lifting its blockade. US forces are expanding their escort capacity, and some tankers continue to transit with transponders switched off. In India, the Prime Minister used his Independence Day address to name energy security, critical minerals and nuclear capacity as national priorities.

DAY 167-168 — THE BLOCKADE BECOMES OPEN-ENDED. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told reporters in Panama that the United States Navy can maintain its blockade of Iran indefinitely, because it will rotate ships in and out as it has been doing, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington plans to inflict further financial damage on Tehran. Ceasefire talks have floundered. Reports on Friday said the aircraft carrier USS George Washington has begun moving from the Pacific towards the Middle East, and CENTCOM denied claims about conditions aboard the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group after more than 260 days at sea. Vice President JD Vance set out Washington's objectives as stable energy prices for Americans, preventing an Iranian nuclear weapon and a stronger US position — a list that does not include reopening the strait for third-party trade. The blockade was lifted for a month in mid-June before being reimposed, cutting off Tehran's main source of hard currency.

DAY 166-167 — RIVAL CLAIMS OF CONTROL, AND A DISPUTE OVER HOW MUCH OIL IS ACTUALLY MOVING. President Trump wrote that the United States has "total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and that the naval blockade is being called a wall of steel. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority replied that the strait remains blocked and will not reopen until Iran's conditions are accepted; on Thursday the Basij commander Hossein Taeb said the waterway is under Iranian control and management. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright then said exports through the strait have neared a seven-day average of nine million barrels a day, about fifteen million from the Gulf including pipelines, against roughly twenty million before the war — a claim that sits well above independent estimates and knocked 2% off Brent. Kpler counted fourteen transits on Tuesday, up from the weekend but far below the pre-war 120-130; eleven took the Iranian-approved route and none the traditional channel, and Saudi and Emirati shippers are reported to be switching off transponders. A senior Iranian source told Reuters there is no ceasefire to extend, because Washington violated the June memorandum within 48 hours.

DAY 165 — MEDIATORS OPTIMISTIC, PRINCIPALS IMMOVABLE, MISSILES FIRED. Simultaneously: a US Navy MH-60 fired two Hellfire missiles into the engine room of the Panama-flagged M/V Vela Nova in the Gulf of Oman after it ignored warnings running the blockade — CENTCOM's running tally is 55 vessels redirected, 3 disabled, 2 boarded. Washington imposed its eighth round of sanctions on Iran this year. Khamenei adviser Mohammad Mokhber said the strait stays closed until Iran's demands are met. Trump countered Iran's reparations demand with his own — naming the USS Cole families and those killed in Lebanon, Syria, Yemen and Gaza — and said it would go into all future negotiations. He also told reporters 'we control the strait 100%', called the blockade a 'steel wall', and acknowledged Iran will 'on occasion drop a mine'. DAY 163 — THE NEGOTIATOR'S CHAIR CHANGES HANDS. Rezaee, 71, commanded the IRGC from 1981 to 1997; he said earlier in August that Iran will never allow an unauthorised route through the strait. DAY 162 — ROUTES AGREED, STRAIT STILL SHUT. An IRGC spokesman called the reopening 'completely independent' of the Oman track. Hours later Iran targeted an ADNOC-owned vessel inside the strait; the UAE blamed Iran. assessment.body:
WHAT HAPPENED
After twice failing to hit a US warship, the IRGC saw CENTCOM destroy five more of its tankers Tuesday, bringing the week's total to eight vessels lost. Rubio's warning — Iran loses tankers for every attempt on US ships — is now an explicit, standing policy. Iran retaliated by threatening tanker crews in Kuwait and Bahrain, widening the conflict's shipping-safety footprint to two more countries. Kpler's data confirms the damage: strait traffic down 28% to its lowest since May.

WHY IT MATTERS FOR INDIA
This week marks a real shift from a market that was cautiously discounting war rhetoric to one that is actively repricing it. Three straight down sessions, Brent at $100, and FIIs turning net sellers together represent the most serious market reaction this tracker has recorded since the war's earliest weeks. The DII buying that's held up through the selloff is the one thing keeping this from being unambiguously alarming — it suggests domestic institutional money still sees this as temporary, not structural.

THE THING TO WATCH
Whether Iran's threat against tanker crews in Kuwait and Bahrain is followed through, which would mark a further widening of the war beyond the Iran-US axis into direct threats on Gulf Arab states hosting US forces — precisely the scenario Qatar's 'industrial catastrophe' warning anticipates. If it stays rhetorical, this week may still mark the moment markets learned to take the tanker war seriously without the underlying conflict itself expanding further. If Kuwait or Bahrain-based vessels are actually hit, that distinction collapses.

Prices still ended the week up about 4%. The IEA cut its 2026 demand forecast by a further 510,000 bpd to a 1.6 million bpd contraction, with 8.3 million bpd of Gulf production shut in. Kpler counted fourteen transits on Tuesday, eleven of them on the Iranian-approved route and none on the traditional channel. The Houthis claimed a drone attack on a Saudi refinery at Jizan. INDIA: Sensex +113.61 (+0.15%) to 78,079.96 snapping a two-day fall, Nifty -40 (-0.16%) to 24,395.85 in a third straight decline, rupee steady near 95.3 on RBI dollar sales, July CPI 4.45%.

Brent closed $88.52 (+1.7%) and WTI $82.40 (+1.4%), reversing Thursday's fall and ending the week more than 5% higher, after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent promised measures aimed at Iran's "economic isolation" that "have never been seen", with announcements expected next week. It followed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's statement that the naval blockade can be maintained indefinitely by rotating ships. The IEA warned of the widest global supply deficit in five years, with supply down 4.3 million bpd across 2026. Iran and Oman still have no agreement on reopening the strait. INDIA: Sensex -70.71 (-0.09%) to 78,009.25 and Nifty -29.85 (-0.12%) to 24,366.00, both recovering from an early fall of more than 300 points; breadth weak at 2,244 decliners to 1,855 advancers; midcaps -0.53%, smallcaps -0.69%; foreign selling continued.

The 60-day US-Iran memorandum expired with no successor deal and no commercial route restored. Trump threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way" of reopening the strait, and narrowed Washington's stated objective to denying Iran a nuclear weapon. Kpler recorded five commodity vessels crossing on Saturday and none on Sunday, against 31 the previous weekend. Al Arabiya reported a ceasefire extension; a senior Iranian official denied any such talks. Brent held near $89 after gaining about 4.6% last week. INDIA: Sensex -281.09 (-0.36%) to 77,728.16 with the Nifty below 24,300; Nifty IT -1.75% led by Infosys -2.83% and HCL Tech -2.32%; midcaps +0.05% and smallcaps +0.36%; the rupee weakened to about 95.67 from 95.42, a fresh war low.

Brent broke $91 and WTI topped $85, the highest since the July blockade week, after Trump said he would not extend the expired memorandum and threatened military action against Oman for a second time. He later posted a map labelling the Strait of Hormuz as "new" US territory, said no talks were taking place and signalled the blockade would be reinstated; US strikes on Iran resumed overnight. Iran's foreign ministry said it had reached an agreement with Oman on future shipping routes, with a regional source expecting a middle ground within days. Kpler counted three ships crossing on Sunday, a five-day average of twelve against about 130 pre-war; CENTCOM has redirected 64 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two. INDIA: Sensex -492.70 (-0.63%) to 77,235.46, a third straight fall; Nifty settled at 24,155 below the 24,200 level on weekly expiry; the rupee weakened to 95.69 from 95.61, a fresh war low.

Trump announced an "economic D-Day" against Iran — economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale — warning that any country whose financial institutions, businesses, airports or government entities provide Tehran a lifeline will face tremendous economic consequences, naming oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries and front companies. The UAE suspended trade with Iran after renewed missile fire. Officials said Trump had threatened to bomb Oman over its Hormuz deal with Tehran. Brent traded around $91.75 and WTI $85.79, the highest of the war. Bab el-Mandeb crossings rose 6.7% to 254 with dark transits down from 40 to 16. INDIA: Sensex -325.78 (-0.42%) to 76,909.68, a fourth straight fall; Nifty -76.60 (-0.32%) to 24,078.30, a seventh consecutive decline, low of 24,025.65; midcaps -0.21%, smallcaps -0.51%; IT outperformed. Asia fell hard — Nikkei -3.19%, KOSPI -6.16%.

Brent climbed to around $92 after President Trump said no talks were taking place with Iran, following the expiry of the 60-day negotiating window on Monday and his threat to bomb Oman over its shipping arrangement with Tehran. INDIA: the Nifty closed at 24,078.30, a seventh consecutive decline and its longest losing run in nearly a year, down 2.1% over the stretch; the Sensex fell 327 points (-0.42%) to 76,909.68, its lowest since 28 July and a fourth straight loss. Power Grid, Bajaj Finance and ITC led the falls; HCL Tech, Eternal and Sun Pharma gained. FIIs bought ₹408 crore, DIIs ₹3,974 crore.

Brent rose to about $93 (+1.5%) and WTI 2.7% to around $86.7, the highest since 24 July, after Washington announced a sweeping package of economic measures cutting Iran off from banks, businesses, shipping registries, cash transfers and smuggling networks, with new sanctions on Hezbollah. The UAE suspended financial and economic transactions with Iran after accusing Tehran of firing ballistic missiles at its territory. EIA data showed US crude stocks up 4.4 million barrels but distillates down 1.5 million to a one-month low. INDIA: the Sensex rebounded 628.04 points (+0.82%) to 77,537.72 after the US Treasury moved to calm bond markets, and the rupee gained 19 paise to 95.57 after fresh war lows earlier in the week. The Nifty rose 153.55 points (+0.64%) to 24,231.85, with midcaps up 0.41% and smallcaps 0.68%; the rupee closed at 95.7050 against 95.7525 previously, with the RBI intervening.

Brent dipped 0.3% to $93.40 and WTI 0.55% to $86.30, but both posted a second consecutive weekly gain of about 5% after touching one-month highs — Brent reached $94.71 intraday. The US military said it had escorted more than 660 million barrels through the strait since early May, and analysis of UK maritime data showed over 80% of liquids using the Omani route with ship numbers at 20% of the pre-war average. Treasury Secretary Bessent promised the toughest sanctions yet and urged China to back them; President Pezeshkian said Iran would prefer to end the war from a position of strength. INDIA: the Sensex closed flat at 77,540.83 (+3.11) and the Nifty at 24,252.00 (+20.15, +0.08%), with Metal and Private Bank outperforming while FMCG, auto and IT lagged; the rupee weakened to 95.72.

The US Treasury launched "Operation Economic Outcast", designating about 60 entities, individuals and vessels for oil smuggling, cyber operations and nuclear and missile procurement, including a shadow-fleet network across the UAE, Hong Kong, China, Singapore, Switzerland and Europe, and widening secondary sanction categories to digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. No country was named and no deadline set; Bessent called it a warning shot. The rial hit a record low of 2.02 million to the dollar. Brent held near $91, down about 1.5%. INDIA: the Sensex opened 109 points higher and reversed to close about 172 points lower near 77,369, with the Nifty at 24,220 — PSU banks the drag, metals the gainers — and the rupee closed marginally lower. Confirmed closes: Sensex 77,369.11, Nifty 24,219.05, rupee 95.75.

Brent fell more than 3% to around $89.26, with an intraday low of $87.65, as traders judged Monday's "Operation Economic Outcast" sanctions to pose less risk to physical oil supply than military escalation would. Oman's foreign minister held Hormuz talks in Tehran, where Pakistan's army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir was also reviewing a map of the strait with Iran's interior minister. Iran's assembly advanced plans for transit service fees, and the US offered $10 million for information on five IRGC commanders. INDIA: the Sensex closed 160.83 points higher at 77,529.94 and the Nifty 41 points up at 24,260.05 on monthly expiry, with healthcare and financials leading; the rupee gained 34 paise to 95.41, its best session in weeks, as crude and bond yields eased.

PRE-MARKET (9AM IST): Trump said the US Navy had cleared all mines from the Strait of Hormuz's main shipping lanes and warned new mine-layers would be destroyed; CENTCOM said over 500 ships transited the southern lane in the past 30 days with about 2% struck. Iran and Oman separately proposed a temporary joint corridor — commercial vessels only, provisional for 30-60 days — which Iran's deputy foreign minister said does not amount to reopening the strait. An unidentified projectile disabled an oil tanker off Oman on Monday night, and Iran blacklisted 45 ships used for ship-to-ship transfers evading its blockade. Trump told Al Jazeera he was "not in a hurry" on talks with Tehran. Brent extended its slide to a third session, down more than 2% to around $86.5. INDIA: currency and debt markets shut for Eid-e-Milad; equities open, GIFT Nifty pointing to a higher start after Tuesday's close of Sensex 77,656.09 (+286.98, +0.37%) and Nifty ~24,335 (+0.48%), the rupee at ₹95.41.

PRE-MARKET (6:40AM IST): Iran's deputy foreign minister said the Oman framework floated a day earlier would close the UN-authorised southern shipping lane rather than reopen the strait. Netanyahu said a diplomatic deal with Iran is "not possible," calling its leadership "savages"; Trump told Al Jazeera the war will continue "as long as necessary." Rubio said the US isn't planning new strikes for now, leaning on sanctions. Regional reporting described a 'busy day' of 20 tanker transfers moving oil out of Gulf states excluding Iran. Brent held near $85.5, a fourth consecutive session of declines. INDIA: Wednesday's Sensex (77,472.94, -183.15, -0.24%) and Nifty (24,207.75, -126.80, -0.52%) gave back the morning's gains to close lower even as India VIX eased to 10.57; currency and debt markets were shut for Eid-e-Milad. GIFT Nifty points to a firmer Thursday open near 24,408, and the rupee — last at ₹95.40 — is expected to open stronger.

(9AM IST, WEEKEND): CENTCOM chief Admiral Brad Cooper confirmed the Strait of Hormuz's internationally recognised sea routes are free of Iranian mines, calling it a "major milestone." Trump told Axios "that sucker is open" and said he isn't interested in negotiating further, calling Iran "begging to make a deal" and June's MOU obsolete. US officials report 20-30 tankers transiting the strait nightly, roughly half the pre-war rate, with Iran hitting about 2% of ships over the past month. Iran's military reached a narrower revenue-sharing deal with Oman but said this doesn't guarantee full reopening. Brent steadied near $88, roughly flat on the week, as Hormuz optimism met a new Russia-Ukraine escalation risk. AP reported US Patriot missile stocks in Europe are 'beyond critical' after six months of war. INDIA: Sensex rose 331 points (+0.43%) Friday on an IT-led rally to close at 77,265, even as the index ended the week 0.4% lower; markets are shut for the weekend, reopening Monday, September 1.

(9AM IST, WEEKEND): Iran's Revolutionary Guard Navy rejected Friday's US and CENTCOM claims that Hormuz is open, calling them "an outright lie" and asserting "complete and decisive" Iranian control — no vessel transits without its coordination, the statement said, until US "aggression" ends and Islamabad memorandum obligations are met. Deputy FM Gharibabadi said the Oman arrangement's implementation hinges on US action, and Iran is "in no hurry" otherwise. Former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei said the strait "will not reopen" unless US forces leave the Gulf entirely. Khamenei urged Muslim nations to confront their "true enemy"; Iran's Cabinet vowed to stand firm on sanctions as the war passed six months. No new shipping data has emerged to verify either side's account since Friday. INDIA: markets remain closed for the weekend after Friday's 331-point Sensex rally; trading resumes Monday, September 1, the first session to price in Iran's rebuttal.

(11:15AM IST): Sensex fell 483.27 points (-0.63%) to 76,781.24 and Nifty fell 171.30 points (-0.71%) to 24,004.35 by 11am, reversing Friday's rally as rising oil prices and US Fed rate-hike concerns weighed on sentiment. Goldman Sachs estimated Gulf oil exports have recovered to roughly two-thirds of pre-war levels (15-16 million bpd, up from a March trough of 5-6 million); Reuters counted just 10 vessel transits through Hormuz on Aug 26, below the 10-day average of ~15. CREA estimated the Hormuz crisis has added $22bn to India's gross fossil-fuel import costs since March ($20.5bn on crude oil alone), a net economy-wide cost of $14.4bn (~0.38% of GDP), and pushed LPG import-parity costs up ~29%. CENTCOM and Iran continue to dispute control of the strait: CENTCOM says "Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz"; Gharibabadi says it "remains closed." The IMO separately reported 6,000 sailors stranded and 19 seafarer deaths since February.

(9:30PM IST, POST-MARKET): Two more tankers — South Korean and Saudi-flagged — were struck by unknown projectiles transiting Hormuz's southern corridor Monday evening, undercutting the US's own 'safe route' claim. Trump said the US would hit Iran "hard" but downplayed full-scale war, calling Iran a "failed nation"; Axios reported a CENTCOM strike plan was shelved before Sunday's Larak Island exchange. Iranian President Pezeshkian, at the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan, offered Iran's most concrete diplomatic opening in weeks: immediate reciprocation with free Hormuz navigation if the US restores its June MOU commitments. Iran's central bank said reserves are sufficient and it's ready to inject $2bn to calm currency volatility. INDIA: Sensex closed -12.99 (-0.02%) to 76,944.28, Nifty -24.60 (-0.10%) to 24,055.80 — a second losing session, but far smaller than the morning's 231-point intraday fall suggested, helped by strong GDP data and RBI rupee support. Brent held above $90.

(10AM IST): CENTCOM completed a broad wave of strikes against IRGC air defence, radar, maritime, mine-laying and communications sites across Iran — the widest single strike wave since the weekend's lull ended. Iran's Foreign Ministry claims a wedding in Sirik was hit, 50+ casualties — an unverified Iranian government claim CENTCOM's own statement does not corroborate. Iran claims retaliatory strikes on Jordan's Prince Hassan Air Base and Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, also unconfirmed. IRGC warns its offensive will continue; Trump warns of a harder US response. Bessent tells the G20 that Hormuz will be 'worthless' within two years as pipelines bypass it. Brent traded above $92, diesel crack spreads breached $100. INDIA: Sensex opened -472.96 (-0.61%) to 76,471.32, Nifty -196.60 to 23,859.20, as Nikkei fell 2.9% and Kospi 3.1%, and US 10-year yields hit 4.81% (highest since late 2023). The rupee opened at a two-month high of ₹94.91 on strong 7.8% GDP data — a notable decoupling from the war-driven equity selloff.

(10:45AM IST): Iran's Red Crescent revised the Sept 1 Sirik wedding-strike toll down to 4 dead (2 women, 2 children) and 60+ wounded, from the Foreign Ministry's earlier claim of 50+ casualties; Vance called himself 'extremely skeptical.' Saudi Arabia confirmed 2 Filipino seafarers killed on its tanker MV Sidr in Hormuz — independently verified. Iran struck Kuwait and Bahrain with drones for a second night, claimed a third round on Kuwait and the UAE, disclosed 7 of its own military dead from Sept 1-2, and blacklisted 11 more ships (56 total). Reuters: Trump aides are working to avoid further escalation before the US midterms; Envoy Witkoff held quiet UAE talks in Sardinia. INDIA: Sensex opened +504.16 (+0.66%) to 76,657.02, snapping a 4-day losing streak, Nifty +37.45 to 23,910.90 — on easing US rate-hike fears (Fed's Waller), not on any Hormuz improvement. Brent traded near $96, on track for its strongest weekly rise since mid-July.

(11AM IST, WEEKEND): Iran fired ballistic missiles at a US aircraft carrier and destroyer; both evaded, no Americans hurt. CENTCOM retaliated under a 'tanker for tanker' policy: destroyed tanker M/T Kylo, permanently disabled M/T Downy and M/T Stark 1 — the most direct US strike on Iran's oil fleet of the war. Adm. Cooper warned of a 3-for-2 cost multiplier for future attacks. Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya command threatened 'more severe' attacks and possible expansion; Trump called the war 'small potatoes.' Dubai crude jumped to near $100, highest since May, as Indian and Chinese refiners compete for spot cargoes. ISW/CTP assesses Iran hasn't achieved its Hormuz goal and may be waiting for a better moment to escalate. Qatar issued the first Gulf rebuttal of Iran's 'defensive-only' claim. INDIA: markets closed for the weekend; Friday's close was Sensex 76,645.88 (+493.02, +0.65%), Nifty 23,937.90 (+64.45, +0.27%), snapping a 4-day losing streak on Fed relief, before this weekend's escalation.

(8AM IST, PRE-MARKET): Iran's Rezaei said Tehran will declare a restricted zone and announce a new Hormuz shipping route with Oman 'in coming days' — a real softening from his position a week earlier. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf warned the same day of a 'heavier and more painful response' to further US attacks, referencing Saturday's tanker destruction. An independent ICG analyst estimates actual August Hormuz throughput at 5-7m bpd, well below Washington's claimed 10-17m. Iran struck at least 13 commercial vessels in August. INDIA: markets open today for the first time since the weekend's tanker-sinking escalation; Friday's close was Sensex 76,645.88 (+493.02, +0.65%), Nifty 23,937.90 (+64.45, +0.27%), the index's longest weekly losing streak in five months despite the daily gain. Analysts flag the weekend's Iran developments as the key uncertain variable for today's session; no confirmed opening print available as of this update.

(4PM IST, POST-MARKET): CENTCOM destroyed five more Iranian tankers (M/T Kaviz, M/T Charminar, M/T Horizon 1, M/T Riesco, M/T Derya) after the IRGC twice tried to hit a US warship — 8 tankers destroyed or disabled this week. Rubio: 'every time they try that, they're going to lose tankers.' Iran threatened tanker crews near Kuwait and Bahrain to evacuate immediately; claimed a strike on Jordan's Al-Azraq base, called 'ineffective' by a US official. Kpler confirms strait traffic fell 28% last week to its lowest since May. Qatar warned of an 'industrial catastrophe'; Iran's Rezaei threatened a full blockade over US sanctions. Brent hit $100, first time since May. INDIA: Sensex fell 813.35 (-1.08%) to 74,764.23, Nifty -203.60 (-0.86%) to 23,431.50 — a third straight losing session, IT and realty leading losses. FIIs turned net sellers (-₹123cr); DIIs kept buying (+₹1,349.64cr). Defence stocks (BEL) gained on ~$11bn in new government military purchases.

brief: The tanker war had its most intense week yet. Wire reporting through Sept 9-10 puts the week's tally at ten Iranian tankers struck by the US, up from the eight confirmed Tuesday, and ten vessels struck by Iran near Hormuz on Sept 9. The IRGC added a new threat, warning it would expand its maritime exclusion zone toward Chabahar, on Iran's southeastern coast.

A tanker crew casualty was reported for the first time this week — one dead, one missing — with nationality still unconfirmed; it has not been added to this page's Indian-casualty count of 4 pending verification. Brent traded above $101 a barrel, WTI at $96.69, and US retail diesel hit a record $5.94 a gallon. A separate estimate put Strait oil flow near 2 million barrels a day, down from 8-9 million bpd before fighting resumed on August 30 — a figure that should be reconciled against this page's existing Kpler vessel-count data in the next update.

India is feeling it through the rupee more than confirmed equity numbers so far: the rupee settled near ₹95.10/USD Wednesday, an intraday low of ₹95.2250, with the RBI reportedly intervening through state banks. Wednesday's institutional flows were confirmed at FPIs net sellers of ₹583 crore against DIIs net buyers of ₹1,509 crore. GIFT Nifty signalled a weak Thursday open, down roughly 62 points.
